name: Amatlán Zapotec
catalog_citation: Riggs, Sylvia. 2011. Beginning Tone Analysis for Amatlán Zapotec. SIL-Mexico Electronic Working Papers #10. SIL International. [http://www.sil.org/mexico/workpapers/WP010i-ToneAnalysis-zpo.pdf, via web.archive.org]
catalog_locator: Section 2 'Background Information', p. 3 (syllable structure/stress paragraph) and Section 3 'Basic Tonal Contrasts', p. 3
catalog_quote: The basic syllable structure is one to three consonants followed by a vowel (which can be laryngealized as noted above) followed by zero to two consonants: C+VC*. Words are principally mono-syllabic. Multi-syllable words are compounds, words with affixes, or loans. Stress on multi-syllabic words is principally iambic. All syllables may carry tone. Some words have historically syllabic consonants that also carry tone (which may or may not be considered syllabic now). This is demonstrated by the word msi eagle which has two falling tones, one on m- and the other on –si and is considered to be one syllable. ... Amatlán Zapotec has four contrastive underlying contour tones: level or low, high, rising, and falling. Tone is not normally indicated in the practical orthography.

audit.recode_to: set by morphology (classification morphological): word stress (intensity) falls on the last syllable of the stem — 'casi siempre.. la última sílaba'; when not final a suffix is present and 'los sufijos nunca tienen el acento prosódico' (adverbial suffixes -ka/-aka, -la, -laka, -pa, -ta, -taka, -tra, -sa, -xa, negative -t, contracted enclitic pronouns -ya/-na/-lu); small lexical/loan residue of initial-stressed words (nesa 'anteayer', nyenlazh 'olvidar'; Mejiko, mispero). Four contrastive tones (A/B/S/C) go to tone_note/the secondary-stress rule. Deciding source Riggs & Riggs 2021 Gramática sec. 2.4 (PDF p. 11) + sec. 2.2 (PDF pp. 10-11) + sec. 3.2.1 (PDF p. 18) + sec. 3.5.1 (PDF pp. 39-40); the exceptions statement 'listed-set' (stated class + lexical residue) instead of 'pervasive'. This matches the catalog's own treatment of tonal Zapotec/Otomanguean varieties with a stated stem-bound stress rule (quio1241 Quioquitani, tilq1235 Tilquiapan, yatz1235 Yatzachi, ixca1245 Ixcatec = morphological); acceptable alternative if the editor treats the suffixes as clitics outside the word: fixed-dominant final final stress hedged 'casi siempre', as coded for sant1451 Quiegolani ('almost always on the last syllable') and coat1243 Coatlán. What should not stand is classification tonal with the primary-stress rule 'No fuller stress rule'.

sources.quote: p. 11, 2.4: 'El acento prosódico es cuando una sílaba se pronuncia con mayor intensidad que las demás. En zapoteco este acento casi siempre cae en la última sílaba. Si no, es probable que haya un sufijo en la palabra y los sufijos nunca tienen el acento prosódico.' pp. 10-11, 2.2: 'El zapoteco de Amatlán tiene 4 tonos: el que sube (ascendente), el que cae (descendente), alto y bajo. ... En palabras de más de una sílaba se indica cuál es la sílaba acentuada con un apóstrofo antes de la abreviatura para el tono de esa sílaba, como en la palabra nkano (BꞋC) cuidar. sources.quote: Front matter repeats the grammar's notation: four tones written in parentheses, and 'En palabras de más de una sílaba se indica cuál es la sílaba acentuada con un apóstrofo antes de la abreviatura para el tono de esa sílaba, como en la palabra nkano (B'C) cuidar.' A script count over the extracted text layer of all parenthesised tone strings with 2+ tone letters and a stress apostrophe (1,540 entries) gives stress on the final syllable in 1,319 (about 86%), initial in 121, medial in 100; 424 polysyllabic tone strings carry no mark. (Regex count, not hand-checked entry by entry.)
sources.locator: Front matter 'Los tonos' (stress/tone notation); entries passim
sources.note: Marks tone and the stressed syllable on every polysyllabic headword, so the 'casi siempre última sílaba' claim can be quantified and the exception class (suffixed/encliticised forms, a few initial-stress lexemes) inspected.
